The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded Pillay the prize on October 9, just hours before Washington imposed sanctions on the ICC as an institution, expanding measures that had previously targeted individual officials. The ICC is now becoming increasingly the tool of the Europeans. In a press statement issued by Marco Rubio, Secretary of State, on Tuesday, the US administration said the action was taken as part of its campaign against what it described as the "politicised" and "unaccountable" nature of the ICC. "The Trump Administration has been clear: the International Criminal Court (ICC) is a corrupt and fatally politicised supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate. We will not tolerate its assault on state sovereignty," the statement said. The administration said the sanctions were imposed under Executive Order 14203, titled “Imposing Sanctions on the International Criminal Court.” "These individuals have directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction," it said. Police have clashed with protesters in Paris as some demonstrations in France turned violent on Saturday. A largely peaceful day of protests turned into unrest after nightfall, as protesters were seen throwing objects and fireworks at police. Around 70,000 officers were deployed across France for a second consecutive weekend and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds. The Interior Ministry estimated around 400,000 people took part in Saturday's demonstrations, with nearly 1,000 arrests made. The proposals were presented during a meeting between student representatives and government officials. According to the students, the measures included limits on the size of certain classes, loans to renovate schools and the replacement of a university admissions system they consider unfair. However, the student leaders said they remained dissatisfied with the government's response and intended to continue their campaign. "Not all our demands were met. We'll go on for as long as it takes,"Reutersquoted Louis Letoublon, one of the representatives of high school students, as saying. The government had not immediately confirmed the proposed measures, while a press conference scheduled to announce the details was delayed. It was also unclear how much the education package would cost. President Emmanuel Macron's minority government faces limited room for additional spending as France's national debt approaches 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). The country's borrowing requirements have also complicated efforts
headlines.llm_reasoning: The article simply reports student protests and government proposals.

headlines.full_text: Macron accuses social media of 'damaging democracies' as cost-of-living unrest grips France Macron accuses social media of “damaging our democracies” and says looting must “never” happen again, as France braces for new cost-of-living protests ahead of its presidential election Macron accuses social media of “damaging our democracies” and says looting must “never” happen again, as France braces for new cost-of-living protests ahead of its presidential election President Emmanuel Macron on Monday blamed social media for “damaging our democracies” as France reels from cost-of-living protests that have turned violent, just six months before voters choose his successor. Visiting Marseille City Hall, which protesters briefly overran on October 17, the outgoing president told members of law enforcement it was “not normal” for the country to be in such “turmoil”. He called for the looting and vandalism seen that day to “never” happen again and promised to “continue to hold the line”. Macron described social media as a “tool for mobilising the worst impulses”. He said the movement would subside if those in authority did their jobs well, by addressing “legitimate expectations” while maintaining order, but cautioned that “nothing is a foregone conclusion”. A freshround of protests planned for the weekendcould turn “risky”, he warned, adding that routes would stay outside city centres to protect public order. Authorities have acknowledged security and intelligence failings that allowed the October 17 violence, which included large-scale looting and damage to public property. They stepped up security for last Saturday’s demonstrations and have promised to remain vigilant. “From a security standpoint, we’ve largely turned things around,” a Macron aide said. Inte
headlines.llm_reasoning: Macron blames *social media* for the unrest, using them as a scapegoat for the country’s problems.

headlines.full_text: Russian forces introduce ceasefire in Kherson direction The ceasefire is part of the preparations for a humanitarian operation near the town of Alyoshki MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. The Russian Armed Forces introduced a ceasefire in the Kherson direction at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) to prepare for a humanitarian operation near Alyoshki, the Defense Ministry said in a statement. "As part of preparations for a humanitarian operation near the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, the Russian Armed Forces ceased fire in the Kherson direction at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 27," the statement reads. Russian Chief of the General Staff Army General Valery Gerasimov announced on October 23 that the Russian Armed Forces would cease fire in the Kherson direction at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 27 to allow for a humanitarian operation in Alyoshki. According to the Russian Defense Ministry, the Kiev regime has been shelling roads leading to Alyoshki and extensively using drones to destroy vehicles. Ukrainian forces have also been using unmanned aerial vehicles to lay mines along roads to prevent civilian evacuations and impede the delivery of foods, medicine and other essential supplies to Alyoshki. Over the past week alone, the Kiev regime carried out 18 artillery strikes and more than 120 drone strikes on Alyoshki and main roads in the area, while Russian troops devised over 300 landmines and other explosive devices. On September 21, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the situation in Alyoshki as critical, saying that food and medicine could not be delivered there amid ongoing Ukrainian shelling
headlines.llm_reasoning: The article presents only the Russian perspective on the ceasefire, omitting Ukrainian context, indicating selective framing.

headlines.full_text: Ukraine-Russia truce takes effect in occupied Oleshky to allow humanitarian aid to stranded residents The truce between Ukraine and Russia entered into force early Tuesday, after it was announced by US First Lady Melania Trump last week. A truce between Ukraine and Russia aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky entered into force early Tuesday, after it was announced by US First Lady Melania Trump last week. Both sides said they would observe the truce starting at 3:00 am local time (0100 GMT). AFP was not able to immediately verify whether there had been a decrease in fighting. And Ukraine's military said early Tuesday that ballistic missiles had been launched toward Kyiv. The war-ravaged city in Ukraine's southern Kherson region has been caught in middle of the fighting since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces at the start of their invasion. Former residents told AFP earlier this year that those remaining in the city were starving, lacked medicine and could not easily leave. The Russian Ministry of Defence said on Tuesday that the truce was in effect. "In connection with preparations for a humanitarian operation in the area of Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, (Russian forces) have ceased fire in the Kherson sector and introduced a 'regime of silence'," the ministry said on its Telegram channel. Kyiv's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said Ukraine was "fulfilling its commitments" to the ceasefire. "The sides are adhering to the agreements that we reached," he said on Telegram. The ceasefire, which applies to a limited area, comes as the Ukraine war grinds through its fifth year. Three-way peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv are set to resume in Novemb

headlines.full_text: Why Israel's election is one of the most important in its history Security and democracy emerge as central issues in Israel's highly anticipated general election, as Middle East correspondent Lucy Williamson reports. Israeli voters are preparing to head to the polls in an election some have described as the most consequential in the country's history. It's the first general election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023. Tuesday's vote could see Benjamin Netanyahu's almost two-decade-long period of right-wing rule replaced by a more left-leaning government. Emerging as Netanyahu's main challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, who says the election is about Israel's identity as a liberal and tolerant democracy. Netanyahu has made security central to his campaign, warning that electing his rivals would risk making Israel less safe. Middle East correspondent Lucy Williamson reports.
headlines.llm_reasoning: It presents the election stakes and candidates' positions in a balanced manner.

headlines.full_text: Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global The next fortnight sees two elections on different continents. The outcomes will shape geopolitics and the global economy, writes James Landale In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world. By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other. Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress. A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global. For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined. The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region. And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy. Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls. Marc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC. But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. headlines.full_text: Gadi Eisenkot campaigns on Moroccan roots in challenge to Netanyahu As Israel prepares to vote, Gadi Eisenkot is leveraging his Moroccan heritage in Likud strongholds such as Sderot. From historical divides to October 7, identity and trauma are redefining the city's political loyalties. Ahead ofTuesday's elections, party advertisements greet people arriving by train to the outskirts of the western Israeli city of Sderot. Campaign posters with various slogans promote the right-wing Likud and the far-right Otzma Yehudit parties. However, one poster is seen more than any others: that of the liberal Yashar party. Its slogan, "Rosh Memshala Dialna," combines the terms "prime minister" in Hebrew and the words "of our own" in Moroccan Arabic. And there is a good reason why Eisenkot's campaign in Sderot and other cities on Israel's sociopolitical periphery focuses on his Moroccan roots. Sderot — located in the Negev desert, about 75 kilometers (45 miles) to Tel Aviv's south and just a kilometer away from theGaza border— is a city with a large Moroccan Jewish community. In recent decades, the city has become symbolic ofMoroccan-Jewish culturein Israel, finding its expression in music, cinema and state politics. headlines.full_text: Netanyahu fights for political future as Israel heads to polls with Iran threat looming Israel heads into a high-stakes election with Benjamin Netanyahu's political future and legacy on the line as voters weigh his security record and the continuing Iran threat. Conservative Israeli commentator Gadi Taub discusses Netanyahu’s record, political staying power and the security challenges shaping Israel’s high-stakes election. Ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 national vote, PresidentDonald Trumpissued a sweeping endorsement of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election bid, calling him a "great warrior," an "even greater partner for peace" and an ally in the confrontation with Iran. The backing could give Israel’s longest-serving prime minister a boost ahead of the country’s first national vote since theHamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, massacre. On the face of it, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has done the impossible one more time - within three weeks he overturned defeat in first-round voting to gain re-election as Brazil's president. It was no mean achievement for a man who before his first successful run at the post in 2002 had tried three times unsuccessfully. When he became president in 2003, he came to office as the first leftist leader of Brazil in nearly half a century. Now aged 80 and with plenty of experience at governing as large a democracy as Brazil, he has bucked the trend of electoral victory for right-wing leaders in Latin America whose policies mirror that of US President Donald Trump. Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty. The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old. He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near São Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s. Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism. headlines.full_text: Brazil’s Bolsonaro drops plans of challenging presidential election outcome According to a report by Folha de S.Paulo, the politician was dissuaded from seeking to challenge the voting legitimacy by his lawyers and key allies RIO DE JANEIRO, October 26. /TASS/. Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost in Sunday’s runoff presidential election in Brazil, has abandoned his plans to seek the annulment of the second-round results under the pressure from his allies, the Folha de S.Paulo newspaper reported. According to the newspaper, Bolsonaro was dissuaded from seeking to challenge the voting legitimacy by his lawyers and key allies, including prominent senators and Sao Paulo State Governor Tarcisio de Freitas. They cited the lack of concrete legal arguments and the unfavorable balance of power for the senator in the courts and warned of new political risks. They called on Bolsonaro to consider the election "a closed chapter." The second round of Brazil’s presidential election took place on October 25. According to the electoral commission, after 100% of ballots had been counted, Lula da Silva was reelected president with 51.79% of the vote. His fourth term as head of state will begin on January 5, 2027.
headlines.llm_reasoning: The article simply reports Bolsonaro’s decision to abandon legal challenges without bias.

headlines.full_text: Defeated Flavio Bolsonaro hands over passports, calls travel ban 'attempt to intimidate' Flavio Bolsonaro says a Supreme Court justice has banned him from leaving Brazil and ordered him to hand over his passports a day after he lost the presidential election to Lula. Flavio Bolsonaro says a Supreme Court justice has banned him from leaving Brazil and ordered him to hand over his passports a day after he lost the presidential election to Lula. Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil’s presidential election on Sunday and has refused to concede, said on Monday that a Supreme Court justice had barred him from leaving the country and ordered him to hand over his passports. “I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also banned from leaving the country,” the right-wing senator said in a video posted to Instagram. He called the move “a clear attempt to intimidate me”. Bolsonaro took 48.2percent of the voteagainst 51.8 percent for incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. The 45-year-old, son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, said the decision to seize his passport stems from a statement by his brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, a former lawmaker based in the US. Eduardo had said Flavio would have to leave Brazil if he lost. “I never said that,” the defeated candidate insisted. Bolsonaro is under investigation over alleged corruption and money laundering in the financing of a biopic about his father. He denies any wrongdoing. headlines.full_text: Fatatu Forest, a hidden natural retreat in northern Iran TEHRAN - Tucked away in the rural landscape of northern Iran, Fatatu Forest is a natural attraction in Khomam county, Gilan province, offering visitors a peaceful escape among lush vegetation, wetlands, rice fields and the landscapes of the southern Caspian coast. TEHRAN - Tucked away in the rural landscape of northern Iran, Fatatu Forest is a natural attraction in Khomam county, Gilan province, offering visitors a peaceful escape among lush vegetation, wetlands, rice fields and the landscapes of the southern Caspian coast. Recognized for its ecological importance and its surviving Hyrcanian forest vegetation, the woodland holds considerable potential for nature-based tourism, although limited visitor facilities remain a challenge. Located near Fatatu village, the forest covers approximately 300 hectares. It is among the remaining examples of the Hyrcanian forests, a distinctive forest ecosystem extending along the southern shores of the Caspian Sea. The broader Hyrcanian forest region, which dates back millions of years, was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2019. Fatatu Forest has also been registered on Iran's National Natural Heritage List, reflecting its environmental significance and the importance of protecting its vegetation and biodiversity. A tranquil landscape of alder trees One of the forest's defining features is its dense growth of alder trees, characteristic of the lowland woodlands found along the Caspian coast. Other tree species, including maple and oak, are found in forested areas around Khomam, alongside plant species adapted to the region's humid climate. The dense vegetation, natural walking routes and quiet surroundings make Fatatu an appealing destination for visitors

Supporters argued that these measures were necessary to confront a transnational threat with legal instruments suited to a new security environment.

Eleven people were injured by gunfire, local police said, while another hurt their ankle while fleeing the scene. Six of the victims were children. Anthony Rivers III, 15, has been charged with 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent. Police said the shooting followed an altercation between people who knew each other and that additional arrests were possible. None of the victims appear to have been the intended targets, they said in a statement. "What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families," Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said. Police said on Sunday that six people were in hospital, including one person who was in a critical condition. Five people had been released. headlines.full_text: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in party The highly secretive four-day Plenum starts Monday in Beijing. A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come. The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks. The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges. The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after. They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year. There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities. The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed. Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite. The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits. Record low turnout in Sunday'sBulgarianelections mean voters are expected to head to the polls on November 1 to cast ballots in a presidential run-off. Polling stations opened at 7 a.m. and closed at 8 p.m. (0500-1800 GMT), with official results expected within 48 hours, but voter turnout was less than 40%, far short of the 50% required. Voters were choosing between candidates with vastly different views of the war in Ukraine and relations with Moscow and the vote came as drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea off the Bulgarian coast brought home the significance of theconflict in Ukrainefor the former Soviet satellite state. Although the presidency is largely ceremonial, the head of state in Bulgaria can appoint interim governments during political crises, is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and is able to veto legislation. Frontrunner in the elections is incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who took over the position this year after currentPrime Minister Rumen Radevstepped down to take part in the parliamentary elections that led him to power. Yotova, 62, who surveys show as having 41-47% of the vote, favors dialogue with Moscow as the way to bring peace to Ukraine and opposes military aid to Kyiv. Former Japanese Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda, who led the country for just one year and spent years afterward trying to build better ties with China, has died, officials said Monday. He was 90. He died on Thursday, the governing Liberal Democratic Party said, without disclosing further details. Born in 1936, Fukuda grew up in a political family in Gunma, northwest of Tokyo. His father, Takeo Fukuda, also served as prime minister and worked to build Tokyo's ties with Beijing. After graduating from Waseda University in Tokyo, Yasuo Fukuda worked for a Japanese oil company for more than 17 years before entering politics, first serving as his father's private secretary just before the elder Fukuda became Japan's leader in 1976. The younger Fukuda was first elected to parliament in 1990, taking his father's former seat. He landed his first ministerial post as Chief Cabinet Secretary, or top spokesperson, for the gaffe-prone then-Prime Minister Yoshiro Mori in 2000. During that time, Fukuda jokingly called himself the “secretary of explanations.” As a lawmaker, Fukuda served in a number of foreign affairs-related roles and developed a reputation as a diplomacy expert. Like his father, he placed great importance on developing friendships with Asian countries. During his 2007-2008 prime ministership, Fukuda developed stable ties with China's Hu Jintao.
